title: De transformatione serierum in fractiones continuas, ubi simul haec theoria non mediocriter amplificatur

deep.reconstruction:
§27 generalises the earlier theorem, which turned an alternating series of reciprocals 1/α − 1/β + 1/γ − … into a continued fraction, to arbitrary numerators. Take s = a/α − b/β + c/γ − d/δ + …. Euler substitutes α/a, β/b, γ/c, … for α, β, γ, … in Theorem I. This gives

1/s = α/a + (α/a)² / (β/b − α/a + (β/b)² / (γ/c − β/b + …)).

He then clears denominators by an equivalence transformation: the k-th partial fraction is multiplied above and below by successive products ab, bc, cd, …, and the whole by a. The result is Theorem III (§28):

a/s = α + α²b / (aβ − bα + acβ² / (bγ − cβ + bdγ² / (cδ − dγ + …))).

This is the Euler-type continued fraction whose convergents are exactly the partial sums of the series (in the form a/s_n).

§29 is a deliberately pathological illustration. Euler takes 1/1 − 2/2 + 3/3 − … = 1 − 1 + 1 − … and gives it the Leibniz/Abel value 1/2. With a = α = 1, b = β = 2, and so on, every partial denominator vanishes:

2 = 1 + 2/(0 + 3·4/(0 + 8·9/(0 + 15·16/(0 + …)))).

The partial numerators are (k−1)(k+1)k² for k ≥ 2. A continued fraction of the form a1/(0 + a2/(0 + a3/…)) formally collapses to the infinite quotient a1·a3·a5⋯ / (a2·a4⋯). Euler writes this as an infinite product that should equal 1. He remarks that its truth is not easily seen, because numerator and denominator have unequal numbers of factors, yet he declares 'no doubt' that the value is 1.

§30 begins a second divergent example: Σ(−1)^{n+1} n/(n+1) = 1/2 − 2/3 + 3/4 − …. Splitting n/(n+1) = 1 − 1/(n+1) and assigning 1/2 to 1 − 1 + 1 − … gives s = ln 2 − 1/2. Here a = 1, 2, 3, … and α = 2, 3, 4, …. The continued fraction, completed on the next page, is

1/(ln 2 − 1/2) = 2 + 1·2·2²/(−1 + 1·3·3²/(−1 + …)).

The purpose of the page is to extend the series-to-continued-fraction machinery of E593 to arbitrary numerators and to test it on (divergent) examples.
errors: §29: the continued fraction with all partial denominators 0 is formally meaningless. Its convergents equal 1/(partial sums) of 1 − 1 + 1 − …, which alternate between 1 and ∞, so it does not converge to 2.

§29: the infinite product Euler derives does not converge. Grouping successive numerator and denominator factors gives ratios (2k+2)(2k+1)/((2k)(2k−1)) > 1, which diverge. Other arrangements give other values, so the claimed value 1 rests on an arbitrary pairing of factors; Euler himself flags this difficulty.

§30: the series 1/2 − 2/3 + 3/4 − … diverges (its terms tend to 1). The value ln 2 − 1/2 is a summation value (Abel/Euler), not a sum. Since the continued fraction's convergents reproduce the partial sums, the continued fraction (on p.156) also fails to converge to 1/(ln 2 − 1/2).

ideas.what: Conversion of a general alternating series Σ(−1)^n a_n/α_n into an equivalent continued fraction with convergents equal to the partial sums (Theorem III)
ideas.modern_name: Euler's continued fraction formula (equivalence of series and continued fraction)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Introductio 1748, ch. 18; De fractionibus continuis papers)
ideas.where_published: Introductio in analysin infinitorum I, ch. 18; E593 itself

ideas.what: Equivalence transformation clearing nested denominators by multiplying successive partial quotients by ab, bc, cd, …
ideas.where_published: Introductio ch. 18 and many continued-fraction papers

ideas.what: Applying the transformation to divergent series summed by Leibniz/Abel values (1 − 1 + 1 − … = 1/2), producing zero partial denominators and a formal infinite product
ideas.modern_name: Formal manipulation of divergent series; degenerate continued fractions with zero partial denominators
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler's divergent-series practice (De seriebus divergentibus, E247)

deep.surprise_reason: Theorem III is the well-known Euler series-to-continued-fraction formula. The divergent examples are curiosities that Euler himself treats as dubious, and nothing on the page appears absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: In both the §27 formula and Theorem III, the second partial numerator should be a·c·β·β (Latin a), not α·c·β·β. This follows from the derivation, (β/b)²·ab·bc = acβ², and from the p.156 example 1·3·3² with a = 1, c = 3, β = 3.

The infinite product in §29 is uncertain in the transcription; it should be checked against the image. The image appears to read numerator 2·1²·4·2²·6·3²·8·4²·etc. and denominator 1·3·2²·5·3²·7·4²·9·etc.
